newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian retail woes shorten odds on rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Australian retail woes shorten odds on rate cut.

text.p: The chances of another cut in Australian interest rates will increase if consumers do not go on a post-Christmas spending splurge, analysts said on Tuesday after the release of figures showing weak retail sales in November and a spate of profit downgrades by retailers.
"In anyone's language, the retail sector was weak in late 1996," Citibank chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.
Retail sales rose 0.7 percent in November, following a 1.2 percent rise in October, official figures showed.
However despite the rises of the last two months, retail trade has yet to recover from the 3.7 percent fall it recorded in September, and remains below the levels of July and August.
"This is an unambigously soft number and confirms the anecdotal evidence that retailers were having great difficulty pre-Christmas," Societe Generale economist Glenn Maguire said.
"Another weak retail trade figure will strengthen the case for a fourth rate cut," he said.
The outlook for retailing does not appear bright.
A number of retailers dowgraded profit forecasts in light of poor trading over the key Christmas/New Year period, with one executive describing it "the worst the company has experienced."
The Reserve Bank cut official interest rates three times last year, in July, November and December, by a total of 150 basis points to their current level of 6.00 percent.
Despite the rate cuts, and continuing high levels of consumer confidence, spending has not shown any sign of improvement in the second half of 1996, and retailers are beginning to feel the pinch.

On Friday, department store group David Jones Ltd said continuing depressed trading conditions in the key Christmas trading months of November and December had led it to lower its earnings forecast for the half year to by up to 50 percent.

On Tuesday, after the release of the retail trade data, upmarket clothing store group Country Road Ltd also announced to the stock exchange that its half year results could be up to 50 percent lower than last year.
Later another clothing retailer, Just Jeans Ltd, also said profits for the half year could be up to 50 percent lower.
Country Road chief executive officer Mike Howell said in a statement that the company had been depending on a surge in Christmas sales after the interest rate cuts.
"This did not eventuate and the Christmas trading environment was the worst the company has experienced resulting in sales substantially below our expectations," Howell said.
Economists said that the continuing soft data across a broad range of indicators, if it extended into 1997, may warrant further action by the Reserve Bank to stimulate the economy.

"Any evidence that retail sales were on the weak side over the Christmas/New Year period will re-focus financial market attention on the possibility of a fourth easing in monetary policy," Axiom Funds Management economist Matthew Drennan said.

Bankers Trust chief economist Chris Caton said after the last rate cut in December he had believed a pickup in growth would obviate the need for a fourth cut, although he had put the chances of such a cut at only slightly less than 50 percent.
"Yesterday's news of falling exports and weak job vacancies, and today's news of continued weakness in retail trade together suggest that we are still looking for that pickup," he said.
